issues.subcategory: impossible test statistic
issues.description: The token specificity interaction analysis in Experiment 2 reports z = 0.60 with p < 0.01, which is statistically impossible. Under the standard normal distribution, z = 0.60 yields p ≈ 0.55. The z-value and p-value are mutually contradictory. This likely reflects a transcription error (perhaps the true z was ~2.60), but as reported it cannot be evaluated and undermines confidence in the token analysis results.
issues.quote: As predicted, the interaction between specificity and condition was significant, such that the target spelling became used more often in the congruent condition than in the incongruent condition as its specificity increased (B = 1.9, z = 2.8, p < 0.01; for the token analyses - z = 0.60, p < 0.01)

issues.subcategory: arithmetic error in suffix count
issues.description: The paper states there are 154 written suffixes in total, then says 64 suffixes were excluded (those occurring in fewer than 20 words), and reports that 95 suffixes remain. However, 154 − 64 = 90, not 95. One of these three numbers must be wrong. This error is consequential because the reported mean diagnosticity and specificity values for 'the remaining 95 suffixes' are based on an incorrectly characterised sample, affecting the validity of conclusions about the ubiquity of these properties.
issues.quote: we excluded all suffixes that occur in fewer than 20 different words in the CELEX database, i.e. 64 suffixes (Baayen et al., 1993). For the remaining 95 suffixes, the mean diagnosticity and specificity values were virtually unchanged

issues.subcategory: inconsistent statistics between text and table for go-past time
issues.description: The go-past time congruency effect is reported with B = 41 and t = 3.837 in the results text, but Table 5 reports B = 43 and t = 3.76 for the same analysis. Both the effect size estimate and the test statistic disagree between the two locations. This inconsistency suggests at least one set of values is incorrect, or the table and text describe results from different model specifications, which should be explained.
issues.quote: There was an effect of congruency on go-past time (B = 41, t = 3.837, p < 0.001)

issues.subcategory: inconsistent statistics between text and table for regressions-out
issues.description: The regressions-out congruency effect is reported as B = 0.3, z = 3.12 in the results text, but Table 5 reports B = 0.25 and z = 2.65. Both the coefficient and the z-value differ substantially between these two locations. The discrepancy in z-values (3.12 vs 2.65) is large enough to affect interpretation of significance under stricter thresholds and suggests the reported values may come from different model runs or contain transcription errors.
issues.quote: The effect of congruency on regressions-out was significant in the expected direction, i.e. incongruent targets were more likely to elicit regressions to earlier regions of the sentence (B = 0.3, z = 3.12, p < 0.01).

issues.subcategory: comprehension accuracy reporting error
issues.description: Comprehension accuracy is reported as '0.86%', with a range of '0.66% to 0.98%'. A value of 0.86% would denote less than 1 percent accuracy, which is inconsistent with a meaningful reading task. The values 0.66–0.98 are clearly proportions (not percentages), and the '%' symbol should either be dropped or the values multiplied by 100. This error also makes the range internally inconsistent with calling it a percentage. While this may appear cosmetic, it constitutes a formal misstatement of a key quality-control metric.
issues.quote: Average accuracy on comprehension trials was 0.86% (ranging from 0.66% to 0.98%).

issues.subcategory: missing denominator degrees of freedom in F-test
issues.description: The test of whether the entropy regression slope significantly differs from 1 is reported as F(1) = 7.44, p < 0.01, but no denominator degrees of freedom are provided. An F-test requires both numerator and denominator df to be reported and evaluated. Without the denominator df, readers cannot verify the significance claim or assess the effective sample size used in the test. This is a standard reporting omission that prevents independent verification.
issues.quote: the slope is significantly different from 1 (F (1) = 7.44, p < 0.01)

issues.subcategory: large discrepancy between raw means and model estimate for first run dwell time
issues.description: For first run dwell time, the raw mean difference between incongruent (389 ms) and congruent (367 ms) conditions is 22 ms, but the model estimate (B) is reported as only 8.90 ms. This is a discrepancy of more than 60% of the raw effect. By contrast, the go-past time raw difference is 49 ms and B = 43 ms. The disproportionate shrinkage for first run dwell time is unexplained and raises questions about model specification, whether outliers inflate raw means, or whether there is a reporting error.

issues.subcategory: non-standard sign-flip approach to combining predictor directions
issues.description: To test whether diagnosticity predicts categorization responses, the authors multiplied diagnosticity by −1 for noun-diagnostic suffixes before entering it into a single model. This ad hoc sign transformation is statistically non-standard and conflates the condition variable with the predictor. The appropriate approach is a condition × diagnosticity interaction term, which would separate the two sources of variance without requiring arbitrary sign manipulation. As implemented, the approach could produce spurious significance if the pooled distribution violates model assumptions.
issues.quote: In order to investigate this statistically, we multiplied our diagnosticity measure by -1 for noun-diagnostic suffixes and substituted this measure in our model, in place of the condition variable.

issues.subcategory: minor frequency discrepancies between Table 2 and Appendix A
issues.description: Table 2 reports the type frequency in nouns for +ness as 1241, but Appendix A reports the type frequency for +ness as 1242. Similarly, Table 2 shows 506 for +ity, while Appendix A shows 508. These discrepancies suggest that different versions of the dataset or calculation were used at different points in the paper, raising questions about reproducibility of the specific values presented.

issues.subcategory: no pre-registration and multiple undisclosed researcher degrees of freedom
issues.description: None of the three experiments were pre-registered. This is particularly concerning for Experiment 3, which tests six different eye-movement measures (skipping, first fixation duration, first run dwell time, go-past time, regressions-in, regressions-out) and explicitly states 'We did not have any concrete predictions as to which eye-movement measures would be affected by the diagnosticity manipulation'. Testing six measures without correction and without a priori predictions inflates the familywise error rate to approximately 26% (1 − 0.95^6). The selection of which DVs to present as primary findings, the decision to conduct follow-up diagnosticity analyses only on the significant measures, and the choice of suffix selection criteria for behavioral experiments all represent undisclosed researcher degrees of freedom.
issues.quote: We did not have any concrete predictions as to which eye-movement measures would be affected by the diagnosticity manipulation, so we chose to monitor a variety of typically studied measures

issues.subcategory: sentence template confound with lexical category condition
issues.description: In Experiments 2 and 3, different syntactic sentence templates are used to create noun, adjective, and verb contexts. Noun contexts position the nonword as a direct/indirect object following an adjective; adjective contexts use a specific set of copular and perception verbs (prove, stay, grow, smell, appear, taste, sound, seem, look, turn, become, remain); verb contexts follow an adverb. The congruent versus incongruent comparison therefore confounds intended lexical category with sentence structural position, verb type, and local syntactic context. Effects attributed to suffix-category congruence could instead reflect processing of different sentence frames, priming from the preceding verbs, or differences in syntactic predictability between templates.
issues.quote: Nonwords in the noun context template occupied the syntactic position of a direct/indirect object following an adjective, and so could only be interpreted as nouns. Nonwords in adjective contexts appeared after verbs prove, stay, grow, smell, appear, taste, sound, seem, look, turn, become, remain

issues.subcategory: significant pre-target word count imbalance between conditions
issues.description: The number of words before the target nonword differs significantly between congruent and incongruent conditions in Experiment 3 (4.75 vs. 5.23 words, p < 0.05). This is acknowledged as a significant difference by the authors but presented as if it can be adequately addressed post-hoc. Longer pre-target contexts in the incongruent condition could independently affect go-past times and regression rates through reading time accumulation and wrap-up effects. The authors' post-hoc control (adding an interaction term) is insufficient to rule out this confound because the confound is structural rather than incidental.
issues.quote: Note that the number of words pre-target was slightly different across conditions (congruent: 4.75, incongruent: 5.23, t(64) = 2.07, p < 0.05)

issues.subcategory: missing random slopes in mixed models
issues.description: All mixed models across the three experiments include only random intercepts for subjects and suffixes, with no random slopes. When experimental manipulations vary within subjects and within items (as is the case here), omitting random slopes can produce anti-conservative tests with inflated Type I error rates (Barr et al., 2013). Given that condition (congruent vs. incongruent) varies within both participants and suffixes, models should ideally include random slopes for condition by subject and by suffix. The authors provide no justification for this model specification choice.
issues.quote: All models included trial order as a main effect, and random intercepts for subjects and for suffixes.

issues.subcategory: single speaker for auditory stimuli in Experiment 2
issues.description: All auditory nonwords in Experiment 2 were produced by a single adult female native speaker of British English. Using a single speaker does not allow generalization of results beyond that particular voice and risks confounding speaker-specific phonetic properties with the experimental manipulation. Standard practice is to use multiple speakers or to treat speaker as a random factor. Additionally, the single-speaker constraint means the critical phonological sequences that should be identical across congruent/incongruent conditions may differ due to contextual coarticulation or prosodic variation.
issues.quote: The nonwords were pronounced by an adult female native speaker of British English and recorded in stereo at a sampling rate of 22,050 Hz.

issues.subcategory: Experiment 1 conducted at end of unrelated testing session
issues.description: Experiment 1 was administered after 'a longer, unrelated testing session', meaning participants were potentially fatigued and their cognitive state was not controlled relative to participants in Experiments 2 and 3. The nature of the prior testing is unspecified. Fatigue effects could suppress sensitivity to subtle linguistic cues (e.g., increasing response times and missing data rates), and the uncontrolled prior task content could introduce priming or interference. The 11.7% missing data rate in Experiment 1 is consistent with possible fatigue effects but cannot be attributed without further investigation.
issues.quote: This experiment was conducted at the end of a longer, unrelated testing session.

issues.subcategory: no neutral baseline condition in Experiments 2 and 3
issues.description: The experimental design compares congruent and incongruent conditions only. Without a neutral baseline (e.g., a context that does not predict any lexical category), it is impossible to determine whether the effects reflect facilitation in the congruent condition, interference in the incongruent condition, or both. This distinction is theoretically important: facilitation would support the claim that diagnosticity aids reading, whereas interference alone would suggest it only disrupts processing when violated. The binary design prevents this decomposition.
issues.quote: For each suffix's target spelling two context types were selected – one that was congruent with the category that this spelling denoted and one that was incongruent with it.

issues.subcategory: lexical category as operationalization of meaning
issues.description: The paper's title and abstract claim to investigate 'the relationship between spelling and meaning', and the abstract uses the word 'meaning' throughout. However, the construct measured throughout the computational analysis and all three experiments is grammatical/lexical category (noun, adjective, verb), which is a syntactic property rather than a semantic one. Lexical category is not equivalent to meaning: 'run' and 'walk' share lexical category (verb) but differ in meaning; 'bank' (institution) and 'bank' (riverbank) share category and form but differ radically in meaning. The theoretical framing overstates the semantic content of the construct being measured.
issues.quote: This paper focuses on one aspect of word meaning, specifically, lexical category (e.g., noun, adjective, verb; see Baayen et al., 2011, for a similar conceptualisation of 'meaning').

issues.subcategory: morphological and orthographic cues not separated in behavioral paradigms
issues.description: The behavioral experiments use nonwords with intact morpheme-like suffix spellings and compare responses across suffixes with different diagnosticity/specificity. However, readers could be responding to low-level orthographic properties of the suffixes (e.g., bigram frequencies, letter cluster associations) rather than abstract morphological knowledge. Experiment 1 explicitly excludes non-pseudoaffixed words 'because the goal of this experiment was not to adjudicate between types of cues used in lexical category judgement.' This means the central question—whether responses reflect morphological knowledge versus orthographic pattern knowledge—remains unaddressed by the experimental design.
issues.quote: We did not include non-pseudoaffixed words because the goal of this experiment was not to adjudicate between types of cues used in lexical category judgement (e.g. orthographic vs morphological).

issues.subcategory: implicit statistical learning claim not empirically tested
issues.description: A central conclusion of the paper is that knowledge of spelling-category regularities was acquired through implicit statistical learning during reading experience. However, no experiment tests this mechanism. All three experiments are cross-sectional assessments of existing knowledge. The claim that 'this knowledge likely reflects an accumulation of experience with spoken and written language' and that it was 'acquired through implicit statistical learning processes' is not distinguishable from explicit instruction, meta-linguistic awareness developed through education, or other mechanisms. The paper treats an unverified mechanistic claim as an established conclusion.
issues.quote: It is unlikely that our participants were ever taught these relationships explicitly; more likely is that this knowledge was acquired through implicit statistical learning processes

issues.subcategory: teleological evolutionary claims from correlational corpus data
issues.description: The paper repeatedly argues that English spelling 'evolved' or 'became fractionated' to 'maximise the transmission of meaningful information'. This is a functionalist/adaptationist claim that requires diachronic causal evidence. The paper relies on Berg and Aronoff (2017) for historical data but does not present that analysis itself. More critically, demonstrating that modern English suffixes are diagnostic does not establish the causal mechanism by which this came about. Spelling change driven by printing conventions, Latin/French borrowing, standardization efforts, and random drift could produce the same patterns without any functional pressure toward meaning disambiguation.
issues.quote: English spelling may have become fractionated in such a way that the high degree of spelling-sound inconsistency maximises the transmission of meaningful information

issues.subcategory: correlational behavioral data interpreted as demonstrating functional use
issues.description: The study demonstrates statistical associations between suffix diagnosticity and participant behavior (e.g., longer go-past times for high-diagnosticity suffixes in incongruent contexts). These correlational results are interpreted as showing that readers 'use' suffix spelling information to 'assist their reading and spelling behaviour.' However, the behavioral experiments cannot distinguish whether readers actively deploy this knowledge or whether they merely reflect passive sensitivity to violations of learned co-occurrences. The stronger functional claim requires converging evidence such as training studies or developmental manipulations.
issues.quote: We have shown that the average reader learns and subsequently relies on morphological cues to class even without explicit instruction to do so

issues.subcategory: no inter-rater reliability for manual suffix extraction in Experiment 2
issues.description: In Experiment 2, the dependent variable was based on manually extracting suffix spellings from participants' complete nonword spellings. This is a subjective coding process, particularly when participants produce unexpected or creative spellings. No inter-rater reliability estimate (e.g., Cohen's kappa) is reported, no description of how disagreements were resolved is given, and no information about how many coders were used is provided. This omission prevents evaluation of the reliability of the primary dependent variable in Experiment 2.
issues.quote: Suffix spellings were manually extracted from whole nonword spellings (1,914 analysable data points). The dependent variable was binary and coded whether the actual spelling was the target spelling for this suffix or not

issues.subcategory: inadequate justification for dismissal of model convergence warning
issues.description: A convergence warning in the regressions-out diagnosticity model is dismissed by re-fitting with the 'bobyqa' optimizer and observing that results are 'identical'. However, a convergence warning may indicate the model is overparameterized, that the likelihood surface is flat near the optimum, or that the iterative algorithm did not find the true maximum likelihood. Identical results across two optimizers do not rule out these possibilities—they may both converge to the same suboptimal solution. A more appropriate response would be to simplify the random effects structure or report bootstrapped confidence intervals.
issues.quote: One way to assess if this warning is a false positive is to refit this model using a different optimisation procedure, such as 'bobyqa' (Powell, 2009). We did this, and observed that the fits of these two models and the significance levels for the fixed effects were identical, indicating that the initial warning was indeed a false positive

issues.subcategory: participant overlap between experiments not addressed
issues.description: The paper does not state whether the same participants appeared in multiple experiments. Experiment 2 and Experiment 3 share some identical stimuli ('some of them were identical to sentences in that experiment'), and all three experiments were run at the same institution with the same recruitment procedure (undergraduate students from Royal Holloway University of London). If participants appeared in more than one experiment, their prior exposure to the stimuli would constitute a carry-over confound. Independence of samples across experiments is an assumption of the cross-experiment comparisons drawn in the General Discussion.
issues.quote: One hundred and twenty sentences were designed following noun, adjective, and verb sentence templates used in Experiment 2 (some of them were identical to sentences in that experiment).

issues.subcategory: participant exclusion criteria not specified
issues.description: The methods sections for all three experiments describe inclusion criteria (native English speakers, no history of reading/spelling difficulties) but provide no information about whether any participants were excluded after data collection, what criteria would have triggered exclusion (e.g., accuracy below chance, outlier response times, excessive missing data), or whether the reported sample sizes reflect the number recruited or the number retained. In Experiment 3, the individual comprehension accuracy range (0.66 to 0.98) suggests substantial inter-individual variability, and it is unclear whether any participants with very low accuracy were retained.
issues.quote: They were native English speakers with no history of reading, spelling, or learning difficulties.

issues.subcategory: missing information about how 11.7% data loss in Experiment 1 was handled
issues.description: Experiment 1 reports 11.7% of data points missing due to timeouts or invalid button presses. The paper does not report whether this missingness was random with respect to condition (diagnostic adjective suffix vs. diagnostic noun suffix), stem properties, or suffix diagnosticity level. If missingness is systematic—e.g., more timeouts for weaker diagnosticity items or for particular suffixes—then the complete case analysis used could bias estimates. Given that the key finding involves graded diagnosticity effects, this is a particularly important potential confound.
issues.quote: We used generalised mixed modelling analysis from the lme4 package in R (Bates et al., 2014) on 1,625 data points (11.7% of data points were missing due to timeouts or button presses that did not correspond to a response).

issues.subcategory: overclaim about universality of diagnosticity and specificity across orthographies
issues.description: Having conducted all computational analysis on English only, and all behavioral experiments with English-speaking undergraduates, the paper claims diagnosticity and specificity 'are characteristic not of the English writing system exclusively but rather reflect general cognitive principles and thus must manifest, in one way or another, in other orthographies.' This extrapolation from a single language is not justified by the data. Shallow orthographies (e.g., Finnish, Spanish) may have very different distributions of these properties due to more transparent phoneme-grapheme mappings. The claim is framed as a logical necessity ('must manifest') rather than an empirical hypothesis.
issues.quote: It is our view that diagnosticity and specificity are characteristic not of the English writing system exclusively but rather reflect general cognitive principles and thus must manifest, in one way or another, in other orthographies.

issues.subcategory: behavioral evidence restricted to nouns and adjectives only
issues.description: Despite the computational analysis covering three lexical categories (noun, adjective, verb) and demonstrating high diagnosticity and specificity for verb suffixes (e.g., –IFY, –IZE, –ATE all have diagnosticity = 1.0 for verbs), all behavioral experiments use verb-diagnostic suffixes only as unanalysed fillers. The rationale given (that 'the majority of verb suffixes do not discriminate lexical category') is inconsistent with the Appendix A data, which shows many verb suffixes with high diagnosticity. This selective exclusion limits the scope of the behavioral claims.
issues.quote: Forty filler nonwords whose suffix spellings were diagnostic for verbs were added so that sentence contexts would be more varied. These filler nonwords were not analysed, because the majority of verb suffixes do not discriminate lexical category (i.e. diagnosticity is less than 0.5).

issues.subcategory: WEIRD undergraduate sample generalized to skilled readers broadly
issues.description: All three experiments used undergraduate students from a single UK university. The paper's title ('Skilled readers' sensitivity'), abstract, and conclusions generalize findings to skilled readers as a population without acknowledging that undergraduates represent a narrow, highly educated demographic. There is no discussion of whether the findings would extend to older adults, less formally educated readers, readers with lower vocabulary, or individuals in different cultural/linguistic contexts. Given that morphological knowledge is known to continue developing post-adolescence, the use of undergraduates as the sole participant group limits the scope of claims.
issues.quote: We have shown that the average reader learns and subsequently relies on morphological cues to class even without explicit instruction to do so

issues.subcategory: diagnosticity conflated with cue validity; distinctiveness claim not supported
issues.description: The paper introduces diagnosticity as a novel construct and states it 'is reminiscent of what is referred to as cue validity (conditional probability of a category given a cue; Beach, 1964)'. The paper then argues that diagnosticity and specificity together are necessary because they 'cannot be captured using a unitary concept (e.g. cue validity)'. However, specificity as defined is simply the conditional probability of a cue given a category—the Bayesian complement of cue validity. The paper presents two complementary conditional probabilities as theoretically distinct constructs without adequately demonstrating that treating them jointly provides unique predictive value beyond what either alone provides, or beyond existing measures like mutual information.
issues.quote: Diagnosticity on its own is reminiscent of what is referred to as cue validity (conditional probability of a category given a cue; Beach, 1964)... Here we hypothesise that the bidirectional relationship between the form and the meaning cannot be captured using a unitary concept (e.g. cue validity), and needs to be expressed through the combination of diagnosticity and specificity (probability of a cue given a category).

issues.subcategory: explicit and implicit knowledge conflated across paradigms
issues.description: Experiment 1 uses an explicit metalinguistic judgment task (asked to decide if a nonword looks like a noun or adjective), while Experiment 3 uses incidental eye-tracking during sentence reading. The paper presents these as converging evidence for a unified knowledge system, but explicit metalinguistic knowledge and implicit processing sensitivity can dissociate. A reader might explicitly categorize –NESS nonwords as nouns (Experiment 1) through conscious rule knowledge while showing different or absent eye-movement effects (Experiment 3). The theoretical framework does not distinguish these levels of representation, and the paper's conclusion treats both as reflecting the same underlying morphological knowledge store.
issues.quote: Experiments 1 and 2 assessed skilled readers' knowledge of the relationship between suffix spelling and lexical category using paradigms that required an explicit response. Experiment 3 investigates this knowledge in a more natural sentence reading task

issues.subcategory: specificity definition conflates phonological rarity with functional specialization
issues.description: Specificity is defined as the proportion of words of a given lexical category that use a particular spelling, among all words of that category with the same word-final phonological sequence. When a phonological sequence is rare (i.e., occurs in few words), specificity will be high simply because there is only one possible spelling for that sound sequence regardless of any functional specialization. Many suffixes with specificity = 1 in Appendix A appear in only a handful of words (e.g., +ante, type frequency 1; +drome, type frequency 2). This means specificity = 1 may reflect phonological uniqueness rather than spelling-meaning fractionation, yet both cases are treated equivalently in the analysis.
issues.quote: Spellings with the specificity of 0 for a given category never go with this category (e.g. –IOUS never occurs in nouns), whereas the value of 1 indicates that the spelling has full specificity (e.g. when a noun ends in /eɪtə/, it must be spelled with –ATOR).

issues.subcategory: subjective trial exclusion criteria in Experiment 3 not operationalized
issues.description: The Experiment 3 data cleaning procedure includes a step in which 'all trials were also visually inspected in order to identify those where participants had not read the sentences in full, or where any considerable deviation in the eye-tracking trace was evident during the trial.' The criteria for 'not read in full' and 'considerable deviation' are not operationalized. This introduces subjective judgment into data exclusion that could produce systematic bias if the exclusion pattern is correlated with condition (e.g., if incongruent trials are more likely to produce unusual eye-tracking patterns that trigger exclusion). No inter-rater reliability for this step is reported.
issues.quote: All trials were also visually inspected in order to identify those where participants had not read the sentences in full, or where any considerable deviation in the eye-tracking trace was evident during the trial. As a result of these checks, 4% of trials were discarded.

issues.subcategory: diagnosticity follow-up analyses conducted only on significant Experiment 3 measures
issues.description: The diagnosticity modulation analyses in Experiment 3 (testing whether the size of the congruency effect is modulated by suffix diagnosticity) are conducted only for go-past time and regressions-out—the two measures that showed significant congruency effects. No justification is given for why these follow-up analyses were not applied to all six measures. If diagnosticity analyses had been conducted on all measures, there would be 12 additional model comparisons, substantially inflating familywise error rate. Selectively reporting follow-up analyses only for already-significant outcomes is a form of undisclosed researcher degrees of freedom.
issues.quote: Further analyses investigated whether the size of the congruency effects on the go-past and regressions-out measures was influenced by the degree to which suffix spellings were diagnostic of lexical category.

issues.subcategory: suffix selection criteria for behavioral experiments allow undisclosed choices
issues.description: For Experiment 1, suffixes were selected based on having diagnosticity ≥ 0.50 and occurring in at least 20 words. These criteria leave many eligible suffixes not included in the experiment (there are well over 20 eligible suffixes in Appendix A meeting these criteria). How the final 20 were chosen from this larger eligible pool is not described. Similarly, for Experiment 2, the 11 suffixes with 'high specificity' were selected without specifying a numerical threshold for 'high'. This opacity in selection procedures means the reported findings may not generalize to other eligible suffixes and could reflect favorable selection.
issues.quote: Twenty suffixes diagnostic for the noun or adjective category were selected (See Table 2). These suffixes all had a high diagnosticity, i.e. greater than or equal to 0.50, and occurred in at least 20 different words.

issues.subcategory: pseudoword generation potentially introduces systematic confounds
issues.description: Nonword stems were generated using Wuggy with a 'CVC structure' constraint, but several stems in Appendix B and C appear to violate this (e.g., 'vup', 'hix', 'guf' are CVC but others such as 'juz', 'tob' are CVC while 'hir', 'til' are CVC—this seems fine; however, looking at Appendix C, stems like 'ræb', 'fɪp', 'ʌft' suggest three-consonant clusters). More critically, all stems were used in Experiment 1 and a subset in Experiments 2/3 from the same pool, meaning item-level properties of stems are shared across experiments. If participants were tested across experiments (which is not ruled out), the same stems appear multiple times in different experimental contexts, potentially producing item-specific familiarity effects.
issues.quote: Eighty non-existing stems with a CVC structure were constructed using the Wuggy pseudoword generator... Sixty-six non-existing stems were selected from the same pool as in Experiment 1.
